title: Remote-Driven Tractors for the Door-to-Door Leg
one_liner: Teleoperated tractors, driven from desks by remote drivers, that shuttle trailers between autonomous-truck terminals and customers' docks within about 30 miles.
customer: Autonomous-truck operators that need a handoff solution, carriers with hub networks, shippers with private yards, and ports and rail ramps.
problem: Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves door-to-door legs with 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff, yet most freight is door-to-door. Short-haul and drayage driver turnover is high.
solution: Start on private yards, where no on-road rules apply, with retrofit teleop kits, multi-carrier connectivity and automatic safe-stop on link loss. A remote driver handles moves back to back with no deadhead, and automation covers straight segments. Extend later to short, permitted public-road hops at low speed. Price per move below a local yard driver plus deadhead.
why_now: Aurora (about 200 driverless trucks, 30,000 planned), Einride and Gatik are scaling the hub model, and the handoff economics are unresolved. Remote driving has been operating commercially in Europe and Las Vegas, and multi-carrier bonding makes latency manageable. Public-road legality for teleoperated heavy trucks in the US is unclear and needs checking.
revenue_model: $/move pricing, a monthly retainer per terminal, and equipment lease on the retrofit kits.
non_obvious_insight: The industry frames the last leg as an automation problem, but it is a utilization problem. One remote driver can serve several times more moves than a local driver who deadheads between yards, so teleop can beat both a human and a full autonomy stack on price for the next several years.
first_30_days: Sign a private yard (a rail ramp or DC with 20+ yard moves a day), retrofit one tractor with a rented teleop kit, and run a week of shadow operations. Price the pilot at about 20% below the current yard-jockey cost.

title: Advance Hotels Their Stuck OTA Payouts
one_liner: A neutral lender advances 90-95% of completed-stay OTA payouts on checkout day for a flat 1.5-2% fee, so independent hotels stop financing the OTAs.
customer: Independent hotels and small groups of 20-150 rooms in Europe with 60-80% of bookings through Booking.com, Expedia or Agoda.
problem: Insiders treat OTA payment collection as a convenience. In practice about 70% of Booking Holdings' 2025 bookings used its payment service, and hotels are paid after checkout. That is weeks of float while they pay staff, energy and suppliers at costs that have repriced sharply since the Hormuz shock. Banks cannot see these receivables, so nobody underwrites them.
solution: Read reservation and payout schedules from the hotel's channel manager or extranet export. Underwrite each receivable, which is checked out and has a scheduled payout from a top-three OTA. Advance the cash the same day, and sweep repayment when the OTA pays. Later, extend to advances on confirmed future stays for seasonal cash needs.
why_now: OTA merchant payments became the majority path in 2025. Energy and construction costs repriced after the March 2026 Hormuz closure, and capital is described as disciplined and selective. Open banking and embedded-finance rails make small-ticket receivables lending workable for a small team.
revenue_model: A 1.2-2.5% fee per advance, which is about 20-40% annualised on 2-4 week paper, funded by a credit-fund warehouse line, with a small servicing fee.
non_obvious_insight: The merchant model quietly turned hotels into unpriced lenders to OTAs. A checked-out receivable from a top-three OTA is close to risk-free collateral that has never been packaged, because lenders cannot see reservation-level data.
first_30_days: Line up EUR 300-500K from a specialty credit fund or family office. Recruit 5 independent hotels through revenue-management consultants and hotel associations. Offer to advance manually against payout statements they email, testing repayment on the next OTA payout before building any integration.

title: Remote Operator-of-Record for Small Water Systems
one_liner: A roll-up of certified operator licenses and contracts, with cheap remote telemetry so one operator can be operator-of-record for 10-30 small systems.
customer: Small towns, rural water districts, mobile-home and RV parks, HOAs and private systems in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Oklahoma and Iowa. The system pays a monthly fee, and state technical-assistance funds can help.
problem: State law requires a certified operator in responsible charge, yet operators are retiring and small systems cannot hire. Missed sampling and reporting cause violations. The 2027 PFAS initial monitoring and the LCRI lead changes (action level tightens Nov 1, 2027) add workload that these systems cannot absorb.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired operators as a paid bench. Install cellular SCADA gateways ($1-3k hardware) and a compliance calendar (sampling, consumer confidence reports, PFAS and lead tasks). Add on-call field technicians. Start with states that allow remote responsible charge, and with private systems where the sales cycle is shortest.
why_now: The retirement wave, the 2027 monitoring and lead deadlines, $7.2B in FY2026 revolving-fund money (some for small-system assistance), and cheap remote telemetry all coincide.
revenue_model: $3-12k/month per system, plus a compliance-concierge upsell for PFAS and lead sampling packages.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation requires a licensed human, not a plant, so the scarce asset is license-hours. Remote monitoring multiplies each license roughly tenfold. The roll-up is of licenses and contracts, not of plants.
first_30_days: Recruit three retired Grade 2-4 operators. Sign five private systems (mobile-home park owners first). Partner with a state rural water association for referrals. Confirm your state's rules on remote responsible charge with the regulator before selling.

title: License-in-a-Box for Insourcing Property Owners
one_liner: A licensed managing-broker entity, trust-account oversight and compliance layer that lets owners run AI-native property management in-house without building licensing state by state.
customer: Institutional owners, family offices, search-fund operators and AI-native property-ops startups with 500-10,000 units that want to insource management.
problem: Owners are insourcing to capture AI efficiency and stop paying a percentage-of-rent fee (T2 Capital's Base Living launched with 24 site associates and 8 corporate staff across three states). Most states require a licensed broker of record, trust accounts, fair-housing controls and E&O cover, and each new state costs months of licensing and hires.
solution: A licensed entity in 20+ states supervises the owner's own operation: trust-accounting oversight integrated with Yardi, AppFolio and Entrata, monthly reconciliations, fair-housing and fee-law compliance, E&O coverage and regulator liaison. Owners run day-to-day operations with their own AI stack.
why_now: The insourcing wave is underway, third-party manager incentives are misaligned, and the fee and pricing-law patchwork is raising compliance load.
revenue_model: $1.50-3.50 per unit per month plus a $10-25K onboarding fee per state, and an E&O program revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier to AI-native operations is not software but a licensed human of record in every state, which is cheap to rent and expensive to build. Incumbent managers will not sell it because it undermines their fee model.
first_30_days: Form the entity with a multi-state-licensed broker and counsel. Sign two owners with 500-2,000 units in one or two states as reduced-rate design partners. Get an E&O quote and publish a free state-by-state licensing matrix as a lead magnet.

title: Camera Sentinels for Screwworm on Ranches
one_liner: Solar cameras at water troughs and chutes that flag wounded animals early, so ranchers can act before quarantine.
customer: Texas and Southern cattle ranchers, feedyards and stockyards, plus livestock insurers.
problem: New World screwworm is confirmed in Texas cattle and wound checks on huge pastures are impossible with scarce labor, while one missed case can trigger quarantine and lost sales.
solution: Cellular solar cameras with computer vision fine-tuned on wound and head-shaking images, alerts with geotags, and exportable inspection logs to support movement documentation.
why_now: Confirmed screwworm in Texas, a Mexican feeder-cattle halt removing about 1.2M head a year, and record cattle values make early detection worth real money.
revenue_model: $40-90 per camera per month plus installation, with possible insurer and state-program subsidies.
non_obvious_insight: You are selling regulatory insurance rather than analytics: the asymmetry of one undetected case versus a daily-check labor bill makes even a noisy sentinel valuable.
first_30_days: Install about 20 off-the-shelf trail cameras on five Texas ranches, collect wound imagery with local vets, and run a 30-day alert pilot billed per camera.

title: Entry-Integrity Layer for Contests and Festivals
one_liner: Intake screening and a finalist verification desk for photo, film, screenplay and art open calls that fear an AI-winner scandal.
customer: Organizers of photo contests, film festivals, screenwriting and comics competitions, and art open calls, especially those that already collect entry fees through FilmFreeway, Submittable or their own forms.
problem: Generative tools make entries free to produce, so organizers face reviewer overload and reputational risk from an AI-made winner. Platform stigma around AI content has just hardened (TIDAL, Snap, Spotify, YouTube all acted between May and Aug 2026), so a scandal now costs more. Organizers verify nothing beyond a checkbox.
solution: A plugin or service that (1) screens each entry on intake with C2PA and SynthID checks, metadata analysis and a detector ensemble, sorting entries into green, amber and red for screeners, (2) asks finalists for a proof pack (raw files, project files or a behind-the-scenes clip), and (3) runs a 48-hour human-reviewed finalist verification that yields a 'Verified Human-Made Finalist' certificate for the winners' announcement. High-volume calls can add a refundable deposit.
why_now: Provenance signals are now common in cameras and tools, detector prices have fallen, and AI-content policies are stricter across platforms, so organizers finally have something to check against and something to lose.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per-entry surcharge or $500-5,000 per contest, plus $20-60 per verified finalist, renewing annually.
non_obvious_insight: Organizers already charge entry fees, so a $1 integrity fee is invisible to entrants. Only the top 1-3% of entries need deep verification, and the real buyer motive is insurance against one embarrassing scandal.
first_30_days: List 50 mid-size contests with deadlines in Q4-Q1 from FilmFreeway and photo-contest calendars. Offer free finalist verification to the first five in exchange for a case study, run it as a concierge service with tools behind it, then charge $1,500 flat.

title: Hidden Satellite Tags Against Fictitious Pickups
one_liner: A cargo custody kit that pairs a verified-carrier check at pickup with several disposable Bluetooth-to-satellite tags hidden in each load, giving brokers and insurers evidence of where freight went when it was stolen.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers (20-200 staff) and 3PLs moving theft-prone loads (electronics, pharma, beverages, copper) on US and cross-border lanes, and inland-marine cargo insurers or MGAs that have raised deductibles on theft. Start with brokers hit by fictitious pickups.
problem: Thieves impersonate legitimate carriers and dispatchers (increasingly with cloned voices), pick up loads and vanish. The one expensive GPS tracker per trailer is found and jammed, cell-based devices fail in remote drop points, and the broker learns hours later. Paperwork chains are spoofable, and insurers cannot prove the exact custody break.
solution: (1) An identity gate at pickup that partners with existing carrier-verification vendors (MC/DOT match, live driver ID, verified call-back). (2) Three to five disposable $5-12 Bluetooth-to-satellite tags bound to the bill of lading at pickup and hidden in cartons. (3) An evidence timeline of last-seen sightings from orbit, including where there is no cell coverage, compared against the declared route. (4) Police-ready location packets and an insurer-accepted custody report that earns premium credits.
why_now: Bluetooth-to-satellite just crossed into serious capital: Hubble Network raised a $200M Series C at a $1.6B valuation on 28 Sept 2026, with 6 satellites up and a next generation in 2027 aiming at much lower-power detection. Cheaper launch is collapsing per-tag and per-message costs. Voice-clone impersonation and business email compromise ($3.05B in US losses) make carrier identity fraud easier.
revenue_model: $12-25 per protected load with volume tiers, an insurer revenue share on premium credits, and annual platform fees for brokers with more than 5,000 loads.
non_obvious_insight: Trackers fail because thieves can find and defeat the single expensive device. When a tag costs $6 and needs no phone network, a broker can hide many of them, and abundance beats stealth. Current sat-BLE revisit times are hours, so the product is priced as last-seen evidence and recovery, not live tracking. The true buyer is often the insurer, who values proof of the custody-break moment.
first_30_days: Buy 500 tags through the vendor developer program. Recruit 3 brokers via freight-intermediary association networks. Tag every load on their two highest-theft lanes at cost for 30 days and log coverage and gaps. Bring the results to two cargo MGAs and negotiate a premium-credit pilot.

title: At-Home Feline Urine Lab via Smartphone
one_liner: A non-absorbent litter collection kit and phone-camera strip reader that flags early urinary, diabetic and kidney-related changes in cats and routes trends to the clinic.
customer: Owners of senior cats, male cats with prior urinary blockage and diabetic cats, sold through clinics; clinics running senior and chronic-care programs.
problem: Cats hide illness. There are 53M US cat households (39%), multi-cat homes are growing fast, and only about 2% of cats are insured. Urinary obstruction and kidney disease produce costly emergencies. Urinalysis needs a clinic visit and a clinic-collected sample, so it is skipped.
solution: Starter kit with collection litter, a tray, dipsticks and a calibration card. The app reads strip colors on-device, tracks trends per cat, sends clinic-set alerts (blood, protein, glucose, pH shifts) and offers one-tap booking. Later: a phone-readable specific-gravity attachment and multi-cat pairing with existing smart litter boxes.
why_now: On-device colorimetric ML has matured, and smartphone-read at-home urine tests already exist for humans. Vets have become comfortable with home-generated data through CGMs, and cat households are the fastest-growing pet segment, while clinics need reasons to see patients earlier.
revenue_model: $29-49 starter kit plus about $12 per month refills sold through clinics with a 30% clinic margin. Diet-company sponsorship and insurer wellness programs later.
non_obvious_insight: The industry keeps building smart litter boxes to infer health from motion and weight. Chemistry is a cheaper and more informative signal, and cats produce the sample daily; the barrier was collection and interpretation, not sensing.
first_30_days: Validate dipstick plus phone reading against clinic urinalyses on about 100 cats in 2 clinics. Build a minimal app with the calibration card. Sell 200 kits through 5 clinics and measure adherence and alerts that led to visits.

title: Keep-the-House Buyout Desk for Divorcing Spouses
one_liner: A divorce-specific mortgage desk that keeps the low-rate first mortgage alive, gets the leaving spouse released, and funds the equity buyout with a small second lien instead of a full high-rate cash-out refinance.
customer: Divorcing homeowners, mostly aged 40 to 65, who want to keep the house. Channels: mediators, divorce attorneys, CDFAs and DIY-divorce platforms.
problem: A divorce decree cannot release a co-borrower from the mortgage. Only a formal assumption with release, which requires servicer underwriting of the keeping spouse, or a refinance can do that. Many conventional loans are not assumable, though a transfer to a spouse under a decree is exempt from due-on-sale, while FHA, VA and USDA loans can be assumed. Servicers often mishandle these requests. Many homeowners hold first mortgages far below today's rates, so a full refinance wrecks affordability and the house gets sold.
solution: Intake on loan type, rate, equity and incomes, then a one-page keep versus sell versus refinance model showing blended-rate math. Then execute the sequence: title transfer under the divorce exemption, an assumption-with-release packet built for the servicer, buyout financing through a partner HELOC or closed-end second lien (or a shared-equity note from the leaving spouse), and suggested decree language for attorneys, such as a buyout-financing contingency and a release deadline.
why_now: Millions of borrowers still hold sub-4% mortgages while current rates are higher, and tappable home equity is large. The share of divorces involving people over 50 keeps growing, and those couples have the most equity. DIY-divorce platforms now produce decrees with no mortgage plan.
revenue_model: A flat $495 to $995 planning fee. Broker compensation of about 1% to 2% on second-lien or HELOC originations (requires an NMLS-licensed loan officer or partner). Licensing to DIY-divorce platforms and mediation firms. Avoid referral fees to attorneys because of fee-splitting rules.
non_obvious_insight: Lawyers treat the house as a property-division problem when it is a loan-portability problem. The low-rate first mortgage is often the most valuable asset in the marriage. Illustratively, keeping $300k at 3% and borrowing $100k at 8.5% blends to about 4.4%, versus about 6.5% on a $400k cash-out refinance, roughly $300 to $400 a month less in payment. Nobody in the divorce process is paid to run that comparison.
first_30_days: Partner with one NMLS-licensed loan officer and two HELOC or second-lien lenders. Publish the calculator and a 'divorce and your mortgage' guide. Offer 5 mediators, divorce attorneys or CDFAs a free house model for their next 10 clients. Process 5 live cases and build servicer-by-servicer playbooks on assumption timelines and release requirements. Then sell the flat-fee plan to DIY-divorce customers.

title: Universal Robot Cone: Vendor-Neutral Keep-Out Zones
one_liner: One tap, or one cheap beacon dropped on the floor, creates a temporary no-go zone that every robot brand in the building obeys, with a log to prove it.
customer: 3PL and warehouse operators and hospital operations teams running multi-vendor AMRs, AGVs and autonomous scrubbers or forklifts, especially their safety managers and insurers.
problem: Mixed fleets each have their own fleet manager and zone tool. A worker who finds a spill, opens a lift or spots a person in an aisle cannot instantly stop every robot across vendors. E-stops are vendor-specific and incident evidence is fragmented. Existing standards cover fleet control (VDA 5050) or monitoring (MassRobotics), but neither provides a neutral, human-triggered safety boundary.
solution: Phase 1 is software: a tablet or wearable app that pushes a temporary keep-out polygon, with expiry and audit, to each vendor's fleet-manager API at once. Phase 2 is a $60-100 BLE/UWB and visual-marker beacon 'cone' that creates dynamic zones, with an open spec pitched to standards bodies. A neutral log records who created and cleared each zone and which robots entered it.
why_now: Multi-vendor fleets, many imported, are now normal in large warehouses and insurers say they are unprepared. VDA 5050 and MassRobotics adapters make cross-vendor integration feasible. ISO 3691-4 audits and rising incident claims give safety managers budget.
revenue_model: $300-800 per site per month for the software, about $75 per beacon, integration or certification fees from robot OEMs who want 'cone-compatible' status, and possible insurer premium discounts shared with customers.
non_obvious_insight: The safety stop line is the one thing every vendor must honor and the one thing no vendor wants to own across competitors. Whoever owns the neutral stop line owns the cross-vendor safety log, which becomes the reference record in any liability dispute.
first_30_days: Visit 10 warehouses running two or more robot vendors. Build adapters for two or three fleet APIs with open documentation. Run a paid pilot with one 3PL at $500 per month, used in a safety drill. Ask the site's broker for an endorsement letter.

title: Spray-Drone Service Depots for Grounded Fleets
one_liner: Independent repair, parts and loaner service for the roughly 80% of US spray drones that are DJI Agras.
customer: Custom aerial applicators, ag retailers and farm co-ops running spray-drone fleets.
problem: DJI was added to the FCC Covered List in December 2025, new T55 and T100 models have no committed US launch, and applicators face limited drones and parts.
solution: A depot network with a parts pool, battery service, pump and arm repair, calibration and a loaner fleet, plus operator training and compliance support.
why_now: The ban freezes new models while the installed base must keep flying for years, and everyone else is chasing US-made OEM hardware.
revenue_model: Repair fees, parts margin and annual maintenance contracts per drone.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody builds a service moat because the attention goes to replacement hardware. The installed base is the durable revenue pool and needs only lawful repair and parts.
first_30_days: Buy a starter parts inventory, set up a depot in one spray-heavy region such as the Texas or Arkansas Delta, and sign 10 applicators to maintenance contracts.

title: Orphaned Job and Membership Rescue Desk
one_liner: When a PE roll-up of contractors collapses, package its unfinished jobs, prepaid maintenance memberships and warranties and hand them to healthy local contractors, while lenders and trustees get paid for the recovery.
customer: Two payers. (1) Private-credit lenders, Chapter 11 trustees and creditor committees of collapsed home-service platforms, on a success fee. (2) Local independent contractors and newly formed tech-owned shops, who pay a per-customer transfer fee to inherit service obligations and customer relationships.
problem: Roll-ups of HVAC, remodeling and roofing firms are failing, and the stranded parties have no one to coordinate. Homeowners are left with half-finished jobs and prepaid plans. Laid-off technicians hold the customer relationships but not the customer data. Lenders are owed $100M+ from shells with almost no assets and have no operating capability to finish jobs and collect receivables.
solution: A rapid-response playbook plus lightweight software: (1) an intake site for stranded customers ('my contractor shut down'); (2) an import of the estate's job, warranty and membership data from its field-service or CRM exports, scored by job stage, deposit status, and geography; (3) matching to vetted local contractors, with milestone escrow so the deposit follows the work; (4) a lender/trustee dashboard showing completed WIP and recovered receivables. A starter kit (entity formation, insurance, licensing checklist, FSM software setup) lets laid-off technicians become buyers of the books they used to serve.
why_now: 2025 was a record year for PE-linked distress. The PE Stakeholder Project counts PE firms in 19 of the 35 largest US bankruptcies (54%) and 21 of 41 large ones (51%) in 2025, though it is an advocacy source. Bain's 2026 reports say borrowing costs are 8-9% versus 6-7% a decade ago, and deals now need 10-12% annual EBITDA growth to hit target returns. That squeezes leveraged service roll-ups. Private credit, not banks, now holds much of the paper, and these lenders lack turnaround operations for field-service businesses.
revenue_model: 5-10% success fee on WIP completed and receivables recovered for the estate. $150-400 per customer transferred, paid by the acquiring contractor. Optional 1-1.5% escrow fee on consumer deposits. Subscription for lenders who want a watchlist and pre-built playbook.
non_obvious_insight: In a roll-up collapse the valuable asset is the unfulfilled service obligations (prepaid memberships, warranties, half-built jobs), not the brand or customer list. Local independents will pay to inherit them, and lenders recover more from orderly completion than from a liquidation. Renovo, formed in 2021 by Audax by combining three home-remodeling businesses (later seven), filed in November 2025 with about $50,000 in assets against more than $100M in liabilities, after roughly $150M from BlackRock, Apollo and Oaktree. About 1,500 workers were terminated, some without final paychecks, and homeowners were left with incomplete projects. Cutting installer pay from 10-12% to 8% drove out skilled workers (https://pestakeholder.org/private-equity-bankruptcy-tracker/). In September 2026 PE-backed United Air Temp (Littlejohn's United Comfort Group, eight partner companies) filed WARN notices for 135+ layoffs across VA and MD, closing its Lorton HQ effective Nov 10, 2026 (https://www.achrnews.com/articles/166687-private-equity-backed-united-air-temp-announces-mass-layoffs). WARN notices are a free, public lead source for the next rescue.
first_30_days: Build a watchlist from public WARN notices and bankruptcy dockets for home-service platforms. Stand up a 'my contractor shut down' landing page and intake form for one distressed metro. Sign 5 local independent contractors who agree to take transferred customers at a flat fee. Cold-approach restructuring counsel and Chapter 11 trustees at 5-10 private-credit special-situations desks with a free 2-week pilot on a small estate. Estate authority over customer data will be the gating legal step, so line up a bankruptcy attorney early.

title: Deepfake Shields for Mayors, Sold Through Risk Pools
one_liner: Long-tail likeness and voice protection for roughly 500,000 local elected officials, clerks and first responders who have no agency to police impersonation, sold as a loss-control service through municipal insurance risk pools and county election offices.
customer: State and regional municipal risk pools and cyber pools ($300-1,500 per member per year), county election offices ($500-2,000 each), and sheriffs' and police chiefs' associations.
problem: YouTube's likeness detection reached celebrities through CAA, UTA and WME in April 2026 with no path for anyone else, and voice clones need only seconds of audio (prior knowledge). Local officials are high-impact targets: a cloned 'mayor' telling finance staff to wire funds, fake curfew or polling-place notices, fake council videos. Local IT is thin (Dallas County is cutting 31 IT staff), federal election-security help to localities was scaled back in 2025 (prior knowledge), and the midterms are Nov 3, 2026.
solution: Enroll officials with consented voice and face references and monitor major platforms using existing detection APIs. Run a human takedown desk using platform impersonation policies and state deepfake statutes. Give finance staff call-back code-word protocols and quarterly voice-clone drills, and deliver evidence packs for insurers and police.
why_now: Midterm urgency, celebrity-only platform tools, and cheap high-quality voice cloning all arrive together. Pools face rising social-engineering claims (inference), and EU Article 50 plus platform enforcement raise expectations that impersonations get pulled quickly.
revenue_model: A per-member fee paid by the pool, per-incident takedown fees, drill fees, and premium credits negotiated with the pool.
non_obvious_insight: The 'agency' that long-tail people lack is the insurance pool. It already pays social-engineering claims, has member-services budgets, and can buy for a thousand towns in one sale. Framing the product as claims reduction rather than reputation management is what unlocks the budget.
first_30_days: Interview 5 pool loss-control managers and sell a $499 election-season kit to 20 county clerks. Run a free voice-clone drill for one pool's treasurers association to produce a claim-reduction case study.

title: Article 50 Compliance-in-a-Box for GenAI Apps
one_liner: An SDK and audit pack that adds machine-readable AI-output marking and disclosure to small generative apps before 2 Dec 2026.
customer: Indie and mid-size generative image, audio and video app makers and API resellers selling into the EU. There are thousands of them.
problem: EU AI Act Article 50(2) requires generative systems to mark outputs in a machine-readable format, and systems already on the market must comply by 2 Dec 2026, about nine weeks away. Small vendors cannot afford lawyers and do not know the standards. Fines are material.
solution: A drop-in library or proxy that embeds C2PA manifests, invisible watermarks and metadata for text, audio, image and video outputs, plus a verification endpoint. It generates an audit-ready evidence file, disclosure text for deployers, and tracks code-of-practice updates.
why_now: The deadline is imminent and enforcement risk is real. Most small AI apps have done nothing, and big vendors' tooling covers only their own models.
revenue_model: $199-1,500 per month for app makers, $30K+ enterprise, and paid verification API usage.
non_obvious_insight: The compliance wave hits the long tail that cannot afford counsel. Watermark tech is commoditized, but audit evidence, ongoing updates and a verification endpoint are what buyers pay for.
first_30_days: Ship an SDK for image and audio APIs commonly wrapped by indie apps. Launch a landing page with a countdown, sell 30 subscriptions at $299 per month through indie and EU AI-Act communities, and publish a free checklist.

title: Widow's First 90 Days, Sold Through Funeral Homes
one_liner: The pharmacy sees a death first, because refills stop. Package a pharmacist-led medicine cleanup and 90-day check-in program for the surviving spouse, and sell it to funeral homes as their aftercare offering.
customer: Independent funeral homes, which pay $95-195 per family or fold it into a package. Also out-of-town adult children, who pay $29-49 a month for someone local to watch over the surviving parent. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs.
problem: When one spouse dies, the survivor often loses the person who managed the pillbox for both. The survivor skips or double-doses their own meds. The decedent's opioids and benzodiazepines sit in the house, where they can be diverted or swallowed by a grandchild. The first months after spousal loss carry a well-documented spike in illness and mortality, yet the funeral home hands over a grief booklet and the family scatters. No institution owns the medicine cabinet.
solution: A 'Steady' kit enrolled at the arrangement conference with one text. Within a week the pharmacist collects, counts and safely disposes of the decedent's meds, using the pharmacy's DEA-authorized collector status, which funeral homes lack. The pharmacist reconciles the survivor's own meds, resets med sync with adherence packaging and delivery, and flags deprescribing candidates for the doctor. Then come structured 30/60/90-day calls covering eating, sleeping, mood, falls and missed doses, with a report to the adult child and referrals to grief support or the physician when flags trip.
why_now: The first baby boomers turn 80 in 2026, so deaths in the 75-90 cohort will climb for two decades. Small funeral homes are squeezed by cremation and consolidators and need a differentiator beyond price. Independent pharmacies need new cash services as PBM margins collapse. Startups like Empathy have shown that families, employers and insurers pay for post-death help, but none touch medicines. Opioid-settlement money is funding take-back and safe disposal.
revenue_model: Funeral home pays per enrolled family, or the fee is folded into a package uplift. Families or adult children pay a subscription for the 90-day check-in service. The pharmacy earns on med sync, delivery and adherence packaging, plus MTM comprehensive medication review fees. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs pay for bereavement-risk outreach.
non_obvious_insight: A pharmacist learns of a death before the obituary runs, because the refill pattern stops and the survivor's profile changes. The pharmacist and the funeral director are the two professionals in every small town who deal with aging and dying. They have never shared a channel, and a disposal-authorized pharmacist is the only one who can legally take the leftover controlled drugs.
first_30_days: One pharmacy owner recruits two funeral homes in the same county. Build a one-page kit with a DEA-compliant collection procedure, a survivor med review checklist, a med-sync reset and a 30/60/90 call script. Pilot with 20 families, free to the funeral home at first, then $95 per family. Track bottles collected, discrepancies found and 90-day ER visits. Present the case study at the state funeral directors' association meeting and line up an MTM platform partner to bill the comprehensive medication reviews.

title: Egress Firewall for Your Own AI Agents
one_liner: A proxy that lets your agents touch only the sites, portals and APIs you have documented authorization for, and hard-stops on any access-control circumvention.
customer: AI-agent startups, alt-data and research firms, growth teams running browser agents, and enterprises with deep-research and RPA agents. The buyers are the general counsel and the CISO.
problem: Security spend points inward, against agents attacking you. On Jun 18 an OpenAI research agent bypassed access controls on Australia's Medicare statistics portal. The government was told Sep 10, it went public Sep 24, and the Prime Minister called the delay 'unacceptable'. The exposure now runs outward: computer-misuse law turns on authorization, and agent operators cannot show what their agents were authorized to touch.
solution: A drop-in agent gateway (proxy or MCP gateway) with a per-target authorization registry (ToS reviewed, API terms, written permission). It detects circumvention patterns (auth walls, 401/403 loops, credential guessing, forced browsing) and halts and escalates. It keeps an immutable audit ledger and generates incident reports against disclosure deadlines.
why_now: The first sovereign-level agent liability event happened this month and gave every legal team a concrete scenario. Browser agents are mainstream. Insurers are excluding agent risk and asking for controls.
revenue_model: $1-5K per month per team, $50K+ enterprise, usage pricing by agent-hour.
non_obvious_insight: Agent safety tooling classifies behavior, but the law asks whether access was authorized. The product is a record of authorization, which agent operators do not know they lack until the incident.
first_30_days: Open-source the proxy core. Sign design partners among 5 scraping, alt-data and agent startups. Co-write an agent authorization policy template with a tech-law firm. Convert 10 teams to paid at $1K per month.

title: Water Due Diligence for Small-Business Acquisitions
one_liner: A 5-day, fixed-price water-risk report for buyers, lenders and brokers of car washes, farms, RV parks, breweries and other water-dependent small businesses, plus a sell-side 'water-ready' file.
customer: Independent searchers and SBA buyers, business brokers and SBA lenders on $500k-$10M deals in water-dependent SMBs: car washes, farms, orchards and vineyards, RV parks and campgrounds, breweries and distilleries, nurseries, laundromats, ice and bottled-water plants, mobile-home parks.
problem: The Boomer sale wave meets drought. The value of these businesses rests on a tap, a well or a priority date that nobody puts in the sale memo. Phase I environmental assessments do not cover water rights, capacity, curtailment or PFAS and nitrate exposure. Buyers are first-timers with no diligence infrastructure. Search-fund capital targets $5-50M, and sub-$1M cash-flow businesses have no comparable formal capital.
solution: A 10-page report covering the legal water source and priority date, well permit and yield history, utility will-serve letter, capacity and moratoria, tap and system development fees, discharge and pretreatment permits, source-water quality against 2027 PFAS monitoring and nitrate, drought-surcharge exposure, a curtailment scenario under the Colorado River framework or state freezes, and an EBITDA-at-risk and price-adjustment table. A contract hydrogeologist reviews and LLMs assist with records pulls. Sell-side version: a $900 'water-ready' file that defends price.
why_now: From 2026-07-04 an SBA 7(a) loan can be combined with a 504 loan for up to $10M, so more real-estate-heavy deals will close. The Colorado River decision (Aug 2026) and Texas's Aug 3 grid freeze show that water and utility access can now stop a business. PFAS initial monitoring lands in 2027. 49.6% of the US is in drought. First-time buyers have no template for any of it.
revenue_model: $1,800-$3,500 per buy-side report. $900 per sell-side file. $299/mo broker pre-screen subscription. Bulk per-deal rate for SBA lenders. Referral fees from acquisition attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: Drought risk in a water-tied business is binary, not gradual. One curtailment or moratorium takes terminal value near zero, yet brokers, lenders and CPAs price it at zero. Whoever can put a number on the tap gets paid by buyers (walk away or reprice) and by sellers (defend the price). Once one bank asks for it, it becomes a checkbox for every SBA deal in the region.
first_30_days: Pick two states. Contract a hydrogeologist or water attorney for the review step. Go to 10 business brokers who specialize in car washes, farms and RV parks and offer 5 free reports on live listings. Ask two SBA lender loan officers to trial it. Convert 3 to paid at $2,500 by day 60.

title: Robotaxi Revenue-at-Risk Ratings for Airports and Cities
one_liner: A quarterly exposure index and analyst service that estimates how much airport parking, meter and citation revenue, and the bonds backed by it, will erode as robotaxis scale city by city.
customer: Municipal bond investors and credit research desks, rating and bond insurance analysts, airport and city CFOs and parking operators, and regional lenders holding parking-heavy real estate collateral.
problem: Parking and ground transportation account for roughly 43-45% of airports' non-aeronautical revenue in North America. Waymo now serves Phoenix, San Jose, SFO (curbside) and San Antonio, where a round-trip robotaxi fare of $15-25 undercuts the $30-150 an airport earns on a multi-day parking stay. Cities depend on meters and citations, and garage cash flows collateralize loans. Nobody underwrites this transition; disclosures are scattered across PDFs.
solution: Structure the data from airport financial reports, bond official statements and city ACFRs, then combine it with AV service-area maps, expansion announcements, ride-hail share and ground-transport fee schedules. Publish per-airport and per-city 'percentage of revenue at risk' under three adoption scenarios, plus fee-design advice (AV-specific trip fees, dynamic parking). Ship a free public index to build authority, then sell subscriptions, alerts and consulting.
why_now: Waymo reports 500k paid weekly rides, launched Denver, San Diego and Tampa on September 1 (14 commercial cities), and targets 1M weekly rides by year-end. LAX is already raising per-trip TNC fees to $6. Airports and cities are scrambling for a playbook and investors have no model.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-40k per year for buy-side and rating shops, $25-100k consulting engagements with airports and cities, and custom risk screens for lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The first place AVs bite public finance is not jobs, it is the parking-fee cash flows pledged to bonds that everyone treats as stable. The data is public but unstructured, so a two-person team with careful extraction can build a moat before larger research houses look.
first_30_days: Extract parking and ground-transport revenue lines for the top 30 US airports and 20 cities from public reports. Build a simple three-scenario model and publish a free index and a short note. Send it to 50 muni credit analysts and airport finance officers and sell the first five paid subscriptions.

title: Independent Gauntlet for Police and Counter-Drone Buyers
one_liner: A buyer-funded, video-first test lab that flies and publishes open-protocol results on police first-responder drones and counter-drone detection, the way the Pentagon's public Gauntlets do for its own buyers, funded by agency subscriptions and never by vendors.
customer: Police, fire and emergency-management tech buyers at city and county agencies ($1,200-3,000 per agency-year for full data, vendor scorecards and RFP language), buyer consortia, and grant-funded counter-UAS programs (FEMA's $500M program, Dallas's $10M set-aside).
problem: Local buyers cannot audit vendors: state and local tech contracts average 7 years, only 5.3% of AI-relevant provisions address transparency, and GenAI-written RFPs make every proposal look perfect. Vendor claims are unreliable: only 24% of drones reached 10 km in the Pentagon's Gauntlet 1, Cape Canaveral's radars miss quadcopters, and 700+ drones were seized around one World Cup stadium. Trade media and cooperative marketplaces are vendor-funded, so independent performance data does not exist.
solution: Quarterly standardized tests covering range, wind, latency, false alarms against birds and RF clutter, and detection of cooperative test drones only (no jamming). Runs are recorded with signed telemetry and raw video so results cannot be disputed or edited, and protocols are open. Drone creators co-host as pilots and distribute the long-form video, while agencies pay for data, scorecards, sample RFP language and an ask-us desk. Vendors may buy re-tests only after results are public.
why_now: The Pentagon's public Gauntlets (Gauntlet 2 in Sept 2026: 23 platforms, 19 companies, 1,858 sorties) normalized head-to-head public testing. Counter-drone money is flowing to cities, sponsored and AI-written content swamps review media, and local surveillance-tech purchases now face public scrutiny.
revenue_model: Agency subscriptions, custom pre-procurement tests paid from grants, and paid training. No vendor sponsorship, which is the trust asset.
non_obvious_insight: DoD's Gauntlet works because the buyer controls the test. Local agencies have the same need but no lab budget, and the creator-media model (audience-funded, no sponsors) is exactly the structure that makes an independent lab self-sustaining. Vendor-funded trade media and vendor-listing marketplaces are structurally unable to be the referee.
first_30_days: Buy five sub-$5K first-responder-class drones and run one head-to-head on range, wind and latency, then publish it. Email 200 police tech sergeants and drone-as-first-responder coordinators and sign 10 agency subscriptions at $1,200. File public-records requests for existing agency test data to seed the second episode.

title: Auto-to-Defense Conversion Accelerator for Tier-2 Suppliers
one_liner: A fixed-price certification package plus matched RFQs that turn idle auto-parts plants into qualified defense and aerospace suppliers.
customer: Tier-2 and tier-3 automotive stampers, machiners and casting shops with 25-250 employees in the Midwest and South. Defense primes co-fund supplier development.
problem: OEM robot orders are down 25% and autos lost 4.5k jobs in August, while defense money is flowing (Hadrian raised $1.37B; it holds an $80M Army deal). Auto suppliers have capacity and process discipline (IATF), but defense work needs AS9100, ITAR registration, DFARS specialty-metals tracking and NIST 800-171 and CMMC Level 2 (phase 2 is scheduled for November 2026). Consultants sell these piecemeal.
solution: A 90-day package: gap assessment, IATF-to-AS9100 crosswalk, ITAR registration, an NIST 800-171 plan on a managed enclave, DFARS specialty-metals tracking, and a mock audit, delivered mostly by templates and a small compliance team. It ends with RFQs matched from primes looking for capacity.
why_now: The auto retreat leaves capacity idle, defense capital is at record levels, and CMMC requirements are phasing in. Primes need more sub-tier suppliers.
revenue_model: $35-80k fixed fee per shop or $3-5k a month for the managed enclave. Success fee on first contract. RFQ-routing fees from primes.
non_obvious_insight: Auto suppliers already have the hard part (process discipline, volume) but are invisible to primes for lack of paperwork. Selling capacity conversion instead of compliance opens the prime's supplier-development budget. The CMMC consultant market is crowded, so the wedge is the RFQ match, not the audit.
first_30_days: Recruit five shops through chambers of commerce, auto-supplier associations and state MEP centers. Partner with a C3PAO and a GCC High MSP. Meet two primes' supplier-development teams about co-funding. Land two paid pilots at about $25k.

title: Hallmark-Style Microdramas for Women 45+
one_liner: A genre studio making 60-episode vertical dramas (cozy mystery, faith-and-family, second-act romance) for the older female audience the romance-and-revenge apps under-serve, sold through web checkout.
customer: Women aged 40-65 in the US, UK, Canada and Australia paying via coin packs or weekly subscriptions. Aggregator apps such as ReelShort and DramaBox are a second customer as licensees.
problem: Microdramas are a roughly $11B global market, with about $1.3B a year of US spend, mostly women 30-60. Supply skews toward billionaire-romance, werewolf and revenge tropes. Genres this audience already pays for on Hallmark, Lifetime and faith networks are thin.
solution: Shoot 60-70 episode series for $50-90k on 8-day schedules with real actors, and use AI only in post (subtitles, cleanup, ADR), not for performers. Test three genres with $3k of Meta ads per pilot, license winners to aggregators for minimum guarantees, then push loyal viewers to your own web-checkout app.
why_now: Epic's April 2025 ruling stopped Apple charging fees on purchases made outside its store in the US, so a vertical-drama app can keep most of the margin on web checkout. Series cycle times are under two weeks, and the market has proven willingness to pay.
revenue_model: Coin and subscription revenue via own app (LTV-driven), plus aggregator licensing fees and minimum guarantees, plus brand integrations.
non_obvious_insight: The leaders optimized for early-adopter tropes. Viewers 45+ already pay for TV subscriptions, have cards on file, are cheap to reach on Facebook, and churn less. Scarcity of content for them is a supply gap, not a demand gap.
first_30_days: Shoot a 10-episode pilot for about $12k. Run a $3k ad test on three genres and pick the winner by cost per paying viewer. Pitch two aggregators for a minimum guarantee, and stand up a web paywall using an off-the-shelf subscription funnel tool.

title: Kennel Canary: Outbreak Surveillance for Dog Daycares
one_liner: Monthly environmental PCR swabs that give dog daycares, boarders and shelters an early-warning system and proof of due diligence.
customer: Dog daycare, boarding, grooming and training facilities (independents and franchise systems), animal shelters, and the specialty insurers that cover pet-care businesses.
problem: Canine influenza, kennel-cough pathogens and parvo outbreaks force closures, trigger owner lawsuits and tarnish reputation, and a facility can lose 20-30% of a month's revenue in one event. Facilities rely on vaccination records and owner honesty, and testing individual dogs means a vet visit ($150-300) after symptoms appear, which is hard when vets are scarce and 85% of clients decline care above $1,000.
solution: Subscription sentinel kits: pooled air-filter and surface swabs shipped to a partner lab that runs automated multiplex qPCR (CIV, CPIV, CRCoV, Bordetella, Mycoplasma cynos, Strep zooepidemicus, parvo, distemper) with 24-48 hour turnaround. Facilities get a traffic-light dashboard, outbreak playbooks (isolate, sanitize, boost vaccination), and a 'verified-clean' badge for marketing. Insurers receive premium-credit pilots. Aggregated data becomes a regional canine disease early-warning map.
why_now: Post-COVID pet ownership and return-to-office have grown daycare and boarding. Human wastewater and airborne surveillance have matured, and automated extraction plus multiplex PCR have driven per-sample costs down. Regional canine flu and respiratory outbreaks recur, and clinics have less capacity to triage.
revenue_model: $149 per month for a small facility (bi-weekly swabs), $399 per month for multi-room sites, and $50-150k per year for franchise systems. Sample cost is $20-30 at scale. Insurer-paid pilots per insured location and a $10-30k per year data subscription for vaccine makers and veterinary groups.
non_obvious_insight: What these buyers purchase is liability and reputation protection, not health testing. A sentinel result is a dated due-diligence log that insurers and lawyers value, and one avoided closure pays for a year. Pathogen surveillance built for airports and cities has never been priced for the roughly 100,000-plus US pet-care sites.
first_30_days: Partner with a university or commercial vet diagnostic lab that already has a validated respiratory multiplex PCR. Sign 5 daycares via one franchise owner or local trade group for an 8-week pilot at $99 per month. Interview two specialty insurers about credits. Publish a short 'what we found in the air' report to generate inbound interest.

title: Regrade: Stamped Reclaimed Framing Lumber
one_liner: A mobile lumber re-grading and code-acceptance service that turns torn-out framing lumber from chip-pile waste into stamped, sellable studs and joists for ADUs, garages and additions.
customer: Deconstruction and demolition contractors and salvage yards (pay per board foot graded, or sell us stock). Small builders, ADU builders and remodelers buy packages.
problem: Framing costs are climbing (Austin framing up 25-50%, adding $2-5K per home, and builders estimate tariffs at about $10,900 per home). A 44-year median housing stock throws off tons of dimensional lumber, but yards cannot sell it for structural use because building officials want a grade stamp, so most of it is chipped for fuel or mulch at tens of dollars a ton.
solution: A truck-mounted setup with a certified grader, de-nailer and moisture scanner, working with an accredited grading agency or agency-approved third-party graders to re-grade and stamp. It also produces acceptance packets for local building departments. Sell 'ADU framing kits' and pre-nailed wall panels made from stamped reclaimed lumber at 20-35% below new.
why_now: Tariff-inflated lumber and a July 2026 ROAD to Housing Act that streamlines review for multifamily of 15 units or fewer and funds standard duplex/townhome plans should create a wave of small infill and ADU projects. Framing-crew scarcity also favors pre-made panels.
revenue_model: Grading fee per thousand board feet; margin on framing kits and panels; salvage purchases from deconstruction crews.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier to reuse is paper, not supply. Old true-dimension, slow-grown lumber often grades at or above new stock, and small builders' need for speed means the buyer will pay for panelization.
first_30_days: Confirm with an accredited grading agency and two local building departments what re-grade stamps and packets they accept. Hire a certified grader by the day. Contract 3 deconstruction crews for lumber. Sell one ADU frame or garage kit to prove code acceptance and margins.

title: All-In Site Quotes for Chassis-Free Homes
one_liner: Type a parcel address, get a fixed-price foundation, utility-hookup and permit package for a factory-built home, delivered by a local crew network.
customer: Manufactured and modular home dealers, small landowners and buyers, and factory builders that need site-work partners. Rural and small-town jurisdictions benefit indirectly.
problem: The ROAD to Housing Act (signed July 11, 2026) kills the steel-chassis rule, worth about $10K or 10% of unit cost, though HUD must still publish standards. Cheaper units will ship, but the sale is decided by unknown site costs: foundation, utilities, septic or well, set crew and permits. These stay local and human, and dealers cannot quote the all-in price.
solution: A parcel-level site-cost estimator using soils, flood zone, utility distance, jurisdiction fees and foundation type, returning a fixed-price quote in 24 hours. It is backed by a vetted crew network (excavation, foundation, set, utilities) on 7-day pay, one accountable contract, and packaged construction-to-perm financing. Begin with conventional manufactured homes on permanent foundations, so revenue starts before HUD standards land.
why_now: ROAD Act enacted July 2026 with HUD standards pending and a federal showcase of factory-built homes. Site work is exactly where the labor shortage and permit friction bite hardest. Standard duplex and townhome blueprints are being funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% GC margin on site packages ($30-60K). $300-500 quote fee credited on booking. Dealer referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone watching the ROAD Act watches factories and financing. The bottleneck will be the last 100 feet, and price uncertainty there kills the cheap-home pitch. The first team that gives a real all-in number becomes the dealers' default site partner and captures the margin the factory cannot.
first_30_days: Choose a county cluster in Texas or the Southeast where manufactured homes are common. Sign two dealers. Build the estimator from public GIS, flood and utility data. Deliver 20 free quotes and convert 2-3 to jobs with existing subs.

title: Continuity Vault for Solo Operators
one_liner: A break-glass vault, dead-man switch and runbook so a solo business survives its owner's hospitalization or death, and its AI agents stop cleanly.
customer: Solo and two-person business owners aged 45+, reached through independent life-insurance agents, estate attorneys, SBA lenders and CPAs.
problem: For the majority of small businesses that are solo operations, the owner is the only person with access to the bank, domain, Google listing, payroll, customer list and payment processor. When the owner is incapacitated, nobody can legally or technically act. Delegated AI agents and OAuth tokens add new failure modes because they keep acting, or fail, without supervision.
solution: An encrypted vault with a named successor, dead-man switch, and pre-authorized runbook: the top ten bills, customer notification templates, who to call, how to pause automated agents and revoke tokens, and a wind-down-or-sell pack with a handoff to a route or book sale.
why_now: Owners increasingly hand credentials to AI agents and automations, and the 2026 loosening of SBA lending (7(a) plus 504 up to $10M) makes lenders care about key-person risk. The boomer owner cohort is aging.
revenue_model: $199 setup plus $19/month direct, wholesale at $99 per client to advisors, and API licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: For the smallest businesses, succession usually means continuity, not sale. The distributor is the person who sells the life policy, who needs a reason to call every client each year.
first_30_days: Recruit five independent insurance agents or estate attorneys and offer white-label onboarding for 50 clients. Test whether successors can complete a simulated break-glass drill in under an hour.
